meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You Have Reached the Pinnacle of Success as Soon as You Become Uninterested in Money, Compliments, or Publicity'?
meta.ogDescription: Wolfe died in 1938; the line first surfaces in 1977, credited to aphorist O. A. Battista. It appears in none of Wolfe's work.

answer.label: Not Thomas Wolfe — actually O. A. Battista
answer.sourceLine: Thomas Wolfe did not write this. Quote Investigator ↗ credits the line to O. A. Battista, an industrial chemist who spent decades manufacturing epigrams he trademarked as “Quotoons”; the earliest citation QI located is Laurence J. Peter’s Peter’s Quotations: Ideas for Our Time (1977), page 455, where it is credited to “Dr. O. A. Battista.” Wolfe died in 1938, decades before the line surfaces anywhere, and it appears in none of his books.

source.excerpt: You have reached the pinnacle of success as soon as you become uninterested in money, compliments, or publicity.
trail: 1966 — Battista publishes A Dictionary of Quotoons. Quote Investigator searched it ↗ and reports the saying does not appear.

1977 — the earliest citation Quote Investigator located: Laurence J. Peter’s Peter’s Quotations: Ideas for Our Time, page 455, credits it to “Dr. O. A. Battista.” QI suspects Peter took it from a Battista collection of the same year — catalogued as O. A. Battista’s Quotoons: A Speaker’s Dictionary (Fort Worth: Research Services Corp.) — but could not confirm the line in a 1977 printing; only WIST places it there, as no. 3962 ↗.
1991 — columnist Liz Smith opens her “Scoop” column with the line and credits O. A. Battista, then aims it at Donald Trump, as QI transcribes ↗.

2000 → today — the credit slips: to Eddie Rickenbacker in Wise Words and Quotes (2000), to Thomas Wolfe in a 2003 Plain Dealer column and the quote databases, and now to Wolfe on Wikiquote, as an unsourced caption ↗.
source.excerptNote: There is no wider passage to quote: the line is a stand-alone “Quotoon,” one of thousands Battista wrote for collections and a syndicated column. Quote Investigator notes it is absent from his 1966 A Dictionary of Quotoons but displayed on the back cover of the 1981 G. P. Putnam’s Sons edition of Quotoons: A Speaker’s Dictionary, a reprint of the 1977 edition.
source.rightsHolder: The estate of O. A. Battista (Quotoons first published 1977 by Research Services Corp., Fort Worth; later editions G. P. Putnam’s Sons)
source.rightsNote: This wording is not public domain. Its earliest documented publication is 1977, in Laurence J. Peter’s Peter’s Quotations (William Morrow) — well after the 1931 US public-domain cutoff, so the aphorism and the Battista collections that carry it remain in copyright with Battista’s estate and his publishers. Short quotation with attribution is ordinary fair use; reprinting the collection is not.

author.name: Orlando Aloysius Battista
author.heading: The chemist who wrote aphorisms for a living
author.bio: Orlando Aloysius Battista (June 20, 1917 – October 3, 1995) was a Canadian-American chemist and author, born in Cornwall, Ontario, and best known in his own field for pioneering work on microcrystalline cellulose — the controlled hydrolysis process he developed at the Textile Research Institute in Princeton opened the door to its commercial use. Away from the lab he was a compulsive maker of one-line sayings, which he trademarked as “Quotoons” and pushed out through a syndicated newspaper column and a run of collections beginning with A Dictionary of Quotoons in 1966. His most-repeated line is probably “An error doesn’t become a mistake until you refuse to correct it” — another aphorism that circulates far more widely than his name does.

misattribution.heading: How this became a Thomas Wolfe quote
misattribution.intro: The line is a documented case of a working aphorist’s work being reassigned to better-known names. Quote Investigator ↗ records two wrong credits in print before the internet finished the job.

items.scope: The name on every quote card
items.why: The earliest Wolfe credit Quote Investigator documents is a December 2003 column in The Plain Dealer of Cleveland, whose author said his quotes came from Bartlett’s, websites and “a few other places.” QI also found the attribution on the quote databases ThinkExist.com and IWise.com. No book, page or letter of Wolfe’s has ever been named — see the full chronology ↗.

Before Wolfe, the saying was pinned on the World War I fighter ace: the 2000 collection Wise Words and Quotes by Vernon K. McLellan printed it on page 255 under Rickenbacker’s name, as Quote Investigator records ↗.

On Wikiquote’s Thomas Wolfe page ↗ the sentence runs as a caption beneath his 1937 photograph with no citation at all — it is not in the Look Homeward, Angel, Of Time and the River, You Can’t Go Home Again or The Anatomy of Loneliness sections. Goodreads, BrainyQuote and QuoteFancy all carry the Wolfe credit with no source line.

misattribution.truthLine: It was written by O. A. Battista, and its earliest documented appearance is 1977, in Peter’s Quotations: Ideas for Our Time, page 455, credited to “Dr. O. A. Battista.” The earliest appearance Quote Investigator confirms in a Battista collection is later — the back cover of the 1981 G. P. Putnam’s Sons Quotoons: A Speaker’s Dictionary; WIST alone places it in a 1977 edition, as no. 3962 ↗.

context.heading: An aphorism about not wanting publicity, published on a back cover
lead: Battista was a professional maker of sayings in a way that almost no one is any more. He wrote thousands of them, trademarked the word “Quotoons” to describe them, syndicated them through a newspaper column, and reissued them in collection after collection. That industrial output is exactly why his name falls off: a line built to be reprinted travels perfectly well without its author.

The irony is hard to miss. A sentence arguing that indifference to money, compliments and publicity is the mark of success was, per Quote Investigator ↗, displayed on the back cover of the author’s own 1981 speaker’s dictionary — a piece of book marketing. Once it detached from Battista it drifted onto a war hero, then onto a novelist, and now sits under Thomas Wolfe’s photograph on Wikiquote with no citation at all.
context.detailsSummary: Why Wolfe is an especially bad fit
detailsBody: Wolfe wrote in long, rhapsodic, cascading sentences — the reader who first put the question to Quote Investigator flagged precisely this, noting that having read Look Homeward, Angel, “Wolfe’s style seems very different.” The aphorism is compact, balanced and list-shaped: three nouns, one clause, no music. It is built the way a working epigrammatist builds, not the way Wolfe wrote.

There is also no location. Every serious Wolfe credit for this line — newspaper column, quote database, social post — arrives without a book, page, letter or date attached, which is the signature of a saying that was assigned to a famous name rather than found in one.
context.pull: A line about not wanting publicity, sold on a back cover, is now credited to a man who never wrote it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes O. A. Battista created the saying; the earliest citation it located is Laurence J. Peter's 'Peter's Quotations: Ideas for Our Time' (1977), page 455, crediting 'Dr. O. A. Battista'. QI also records: the saying is absent from Battista's 1966 'A Dictionary of Quotoons'; it appears on the back cover of the 1981 G. P. Putnam's Sons edition of 'Quotoons: A Speaker's Dictionary' (a reprint of the 1977 Research Services Corp., Fort Worth edition); Liz Smith credited Battista in her 1991 'Scoop' column with a Donald Trump barb; 'Wise Words and Quotes' (2000), p. 255, credited Eddie Rickenbacker; a 14 December 2003 column in The Plain Dealer (Cleveland) credited Thomas Wolfe; and ThinkExist.com and IWise.com credited Wolfe.

WIST attributes the exact wording to Orlando A. Battista (1917-1995), 'Canadian-American chemist, aphorist', cites 'Quotoons: A Speaker's Dictionary, No. 3962 (1977 ed.)', and states it is 'Often misattributed to Thomas Wolfe.'

Wikipedia states Orlando Aloysius Battista (June 20, 1917 - October 3, 1995) was a Canadian-American chemist and author, born in Cornwall, Ontario; that his work at the Textile Research Institute, Princeton, obtained microcrystalline cellulose by controlled hydrolysis and opened the door to its commercialisation; that he is associated with the aphorism 'An error doesn't become a mistake until you refuse to correct it'; and lists 'O. A. Battista's Quotations: A Speaker's Dictionary' (1977) among his books.

Wikiquote's Thomas Wolfe page carries 'You have reached the pinnacle of success as soon as you become uninterested in money, compliments, or publicity' as an unsourced caption on the Thomas Wolfe 1937 photograph at the very top of the page, with no citation, and it does not appear in any of the page's sourced sections (Look Homeward, Angel; Of Time and the River; You Can't Go Home Again; The Anatomy of Loneliness). The page gives Wolfe's dates as October 3, 1900 - September 15, 1938.
Open Library holds a catalogue record for 'O. A. Battista's Quotoons' by O. A. Battista, first published 1977, publisher Research Services Corp., Book Pub. Division.
The Internet Archive holds a copy of 'Peter's quotations: ideas for our time' by Laurence J. Peter dated 1977 - the compilation containing the earliest citation Quote Investigator located.
